title.narrative: Supporting competency-based education reforms in the region

description.narrative: All five Central Asian states—Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan—are actively transitioning from traditional, knowledge-based education models to competency-based education (CBE). This region-wide shift aims to align national systems with global standards, address 21st-century skill demands, and respond to dynamic labor market requirements. While each country is at a different stage of implementation, they face a shared set of challenges and needs, particularly in the areas of curricula and policy. Despite differing national contexts, Central Asian states share several critical needs in curriculum development: 1. Moving from content overload to flexible outcomes: All countries struggle with curricula inherited from the Soviet-era that are content-heavy and emphasize rote memorization. The region needs flexible, regularly updated curricula focused on measurable learning outcomes and practical application. 2. Integrating cross-cutting competencies: Curricula must systematically incorporate 21st-century skills, including: o Digital literacy and ICT competencies o Critical thinking and problem-solving o Socio-emotional learning o Green competencies and climate resilience o Transversal and meta-cognitive skills 3. Developing competency-based learning materials: The region requires new textbooks, teacher guides, and assessment tools that move away from traditional testing toward performance-based and portfolio assessments. 4. Strengthening work-based and lifelong learning: Curricula at secondary and tertiary levels need structured integration of work-based learning, employer partnerships, modular programs, and micro-credentials to support lifelong learning. UNESCO Almaty RO plans to assist regional education policymakers through Sector-wide Policies and Plans, EMIS, Curriculum, and Learning Assessments in enabling CBE reform by providing technical advice in 1)creating coherent national assessment systems aligned with competency-based outcomes; 2) adopting teacher professional standards backed by sustainable continuous professional development (CPD) systems, including in-service training centers and digital upskilling; 3) bridging policy-practice gaps by developing policies that would include implementation roadmaps, school-level support, and mechanisms to shift teacher mindsets from traditional instruction to facilitative, competency-based pedagogies; 4)setting standards in greening education and AI in education, as newly emerging areas of education.
